1016.title: Ambedkar's vows
1016.hook: his twenty-two vows, and a Buddhism centered on equality
1016.howItsDone: At conversion ceremonies in the Ambedkarite tradition, new Buddhists take the three refuges and the five precepts and then recite Ambedkar's twenty-two vows together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambedkar's conversion: the refuges at Nagpur, led by one of the crowd's own. Your line was dignity chosen. Whose story did you tell? Day one thousand sixteen.

After the refuges, Ambedkar didn't step down. The crowd was still standing on the open ground in Nagpur. He read out a list of vows and asked them to take every one with him, line by line. Twenty-two of them. Some sound like what anyone taking refuge might promise: keep the precepts, follow the eightfold path. Others are sharp, and meant to be. Running through the whole list, like a spine, is one idea: every person is equal. Today's word: Ambedkar's vows.
screen: `A LIST OF VOWS.` → `SOME FAMILIAR, SOME SHARP.` → `ONE SPINE: EQUAL.`

segments.voice: First, the vows that turn away. A number of them ask his followers to leave behind the gods, rites and caste customs of the faith they had been born into. Those vows were written for his own followers, out of his own history and theirs, and Hindu readers may see them very differently. Here we simply say what they say, and judge no one. Second, the vows that turn toward. Others commit to the Buddha's teaching: to keep the precepts, not to kill, not to steal, not to lie, to practice compassion and loving-kindness, and to walk the eightfold path. These would sound familiar in a monastery in Burma or Thailand. Third, rivers into the ocean. Among the vows is a plain statement that all people are equal, and a promise to work to make that true. There's an old picture in the Pali texts that fits it. The Buddha compares the great rivers that flow into the ocean and lose their names there to people of every caste who join his order: once inside, the old names no longer count. Ambedkar read the Buddha's community in that spirit, as a place where caste dissolves. Fourth, a Buddhism for now. His followers sometimes call this reading Navayana, a new vehicle. It reads the Buddha's path as freedom inside the mind and also freedom in society. Some Buddhists of other schools question parts of his reinterpretation; his followers hear in it the Buddha speaking straight into their lives. Either way, in these vows equality isn't only a feeling. It's a promise you say out loud.
screen: `SOME VOWS TURN AWAY.` · `SOME VOWS TURN TOWARD.` · `RIVERS LOSE THEIR NAMES.` · `EQUALITY AS A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rivers into the ocean. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind three people: someone you look up to, someone you barely notice, and someone you find hard. See each of them as a river, with its own name, running toward the same wide sea. With each out-breath, let the names soften, and let all three rest level in the water. You don't have to like them all. Just see them as equal for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Ambedkar's vows. The twenty-two vows he gave at Nagpur, turning away from caste and toward the Buddha's path, with equality running through them. Today's word.
Your line: equal. Today, treat everyone as equal: the same tone for the cleaner and the boss, the same patience for the stranger and the friend. Day one thousand sixteen.

1017.title: The nuns return
1017.hook: since the late twentieth century, full ordination for women has been renewed in several lineages; views on it differ
1017.carry: taking the old story at its word
1017.howItsDone: In some Theravada and Mahayana communities women now receive full bhikkhuni ordination from monks and nuns together; in others women live as eight- or ten-precept nuns, and the question of renewal is discussed openly and settled differently by different communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ambedkar's vows, and a Buddhism built on equality. Your line: equal. Where did you catch yourself sorting people into higher and lower? Day one thousand seventeen.

Shaved heads, robes the color of turmeric, a line of women walking slowly into an ordination hall while monks wait inside to receive them. Scenes like this have happened in Sri Lanka, in Thailand, in the West, and each one has made news inside the Buddhist world. Why? Women have shaved their heads and kept precepts in Buddhist countries for a long time. But being a fully ordained nun, a bhikkhuni, is something else. In some lineages that order had disappeared, and nobody alive could pass it on. Today is about what happened when women went looking for a way back.
screen: `WOMEN WALK INTO THE HALL.` → `WHY IS THIS NEWS?` → `A LINE THAT HAD BROKEN.`

segments.voice: Start with the old story. In the Vinaya, the monastic rulebook, Mahapajapati, the woman who raised the Buddha, asks him to let women go forth. He hesitates. She and other women cut their hair, put on robes and follow him anyway, on foot, until their feet are swollen and dusty. Ananda speaks for them and asks the Buddha whether women can reach awakening. The Buddha says they can. So the order of nuns begins, with extra rules that place the nuns under the monks. Here's the difficulty. Full ordination is handed on by people who already have it, monks and nuns together. In the Theravada lands, the nuns' order died out or never took firm root, and in Tibet it seems never to have been brought in at all. Women kept practicing, as eight-precept or ten-precept nuns, but without full ordination. Then, in our own time, women from Sri Lanka, Thailand and elsewhere received full ordination, sometimes with help from Chinese and Korean nuns, whose line had continued. Views on this differ, and the people who hold them are sincere. Some Theravada monks and scholars say a broken line can't be restored from outside, so these ordinations don't count under the rules. Others say the Buddha himself opened the door to women, and the rules allow it to be opened again. Tibetan teachers have studied the question at length. Some nuns are glad to keep their present vows and want no change. It's a real argument about how to keep faith with rules handed down from teacher to student. And whatever any monastery decides, the women walking into those halls are taking the old story at its word.
screen: `MAHAPAJAPATI ASKS TO GO FORTH.` · `ORDINATION PASSES PERSON TO PERSON.` · `THE NUNS' LINE BREAKS, THEN RETURNS.` · `SINCERE VIEWS ON BOTH SIDES.` · then, large: `WOMEN CAN AWAKEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: honor a woman who ordained. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind Mahapajapati on that long road, her feet sore, still walking. Or a nun you've read about or met, or a woman in any tradition who gave her life to practice when it wasn't easy. You don't need her name. Just hold the picture: someone who went forth. Let a little respect rise for her, the way you'd stand when someone walks into a room. When the mind wanders, come back to her steps. The bell holds the time.
Bhikkhuni. The full ordination for women, lost in some lineages and renewed in some, while sincere teachers still differ about it. Today's words.
Your line: taking the old story at its word. Today, find the name of one Buddhist nun, living or long ago, and read one thing she said. Day one thousand seventeen.

1018.title: Dipa Ma
1018.hook: the Indian laywoman who lost her family, found peace through meditation, and taught many
1018.howItsDone: Insight meditation teachers often tell Dipa Ma's story as an example of a householder's practice, and some retreat centers and sitting groups encourage people to bring noting into chores, cooking and caring for family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, women walking back into the ordination hall. Your line: taking the old story at its word. Did you find a nun's name, and one thing she said? Day one thousand eighteen.

A small woman in a white sari sits in a cramped apartment in Calcutta. Her visitors are students, neighbors, sometimes Westerners who have traveled a long way. She isn't a nun. She has no temple. She cooks, she looks after her grandson, and she teaches meditation from the floor of her home. Years earlier, people who knew her say, grief had left her so weak she could barely climb the steps of a temple. Today is the story of how she got from there to here.
screen: `A WHITE SARI, A SMALL APARTMENT.` → `NO TEMPLE, NO ROBES.` → `ONCE TOO WEAK TO CLIMB THE STEPS.`

segments.voice: Her name was Nani Bala Barua, and people came to call her Dipa Ma, mother of Dipa, after her daughter. She grew up in a Buddhist family in Bengal, married, and moved with her husband to Burma. Then the losses came, one after another, as her students tell it: children who died, and then her husband. She was left with her young daughter Dipa, with grief, and with a body that was failing. A doctor, the story goes, told her that her real illness was sorrow, and that she should learn to meditate. So she went to a meditation center in Rangoon. The early days were hard. Her students tell how, on her way to the center, she would stop and stop, and finally crawl up the stairs. But she kept going. She practiced with the method of noting, naming each movement of body and mind as it happened, and over time, her students say, the grief loosened its hold and her health came back. Later she moved to Calcutta and taught there, mostly to householders like herself: mothers, workers, people who couldn't leave for a monastery. Some of the teachers who later brought insight meditation to the West studied with her. What she told them was plain. Practice in the kitchen. Practice while you cook, while you wash, while you look after a child. You don't need a cave. The thing worth remembering is the order of the story. She didn't heal first and then practice. She practiced while she was broken, and rebuilt from there, one noted step at a time.
screen: `NANI BALA BARUA, CALLED DIPA MA.` · `LOSS AFTER LOSS, THEN ILLNESS.` · `CRAWLING UP THE STAIRS TO PRACTICE.` · `TEACHING HOUSEHOLDERS IN CALCUTTA.` · then, large: `PRACTICE IN THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: honor someone who rebuilt. Sit, and let the breath come and go. Bring to mind a person you know who went through something hard and slowly put a life back together. A grandparent, a friend, a neighbor, maybe you. Don't tell the whole story to yourself. Just picture them on an ordinary day afterward: making breakfast, going to work, laughing at something small. Let the respect be quiet. If your mind drifts, note it, wandering, and come back to their face. The bell holds the time.
Dipa Ma. A laywoman who practiced through grief, rebuilt her life, and taught householders to meditate right where they lived. Today's word.
Your line: she rebuilt. Today, while you do one chore, washing up, folding, cooking, give it your full attention the way Dipa Ma taught. Day one thousand eighteen.

1019.title: Engaged Buddhism
1019.hook: Thich Nhat Hanh and others bring practice to war, peace and daily life
1019.howItsDone: Engaged Buddhist groups run prison meditation programs, hospice care, disaster relief and peace work, and communities in the Plum Village tradition practice mindful breathing and walking alongside their service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dipa Ma, practicing through grief and teaching from her kitchen floor. Your line: she rebuilt. Which chore did you give your full attention? Day one thousand nineteen.

A temple bell rings for evening sitting. Outside, not far off, there's the sound of planes, and smoke over a village. Inside the temple, young monks look at each other. This was Vietnam during the war, and the question in that room was not abstract. Do you stay on the cushion, where the practice is? Or do you go out to the village, where the people are? A monk named Thich Nhat Hanh spent his life answering that question, and the answer gave a name to a whole movement.
screen: `A BELL, AND SMOKE OVER A VILLAGE.` → `STAY ON THE CUSHION?` → `OR GO OUT?`

segments.voice: Thich Nhat Hanh was a Vietnamese Zen monk. As he told it later, when bombs were falling, monks and nuns had to choose between meditating in the monastery and going out to help the wounded. He said they chose both. They went out to rebuild villages and care for people, and they tried to keep their mindfulness while they did it, breathing as they carried the injured, walking with attention through the ruins. He called this engaged Buddhism: practice that doesn't stop at the temple door. He started a school of young social workers who went into the villages. He spoke against the war and was barred from going home, and he lived much of his life in exile, teaching in France. He was not the only one. Teachers in other countries have brought the practice into prisons, hospitals, protests, refugee camps and kitchens, each in their own way. And here's the turn that keeps engaged Buddhism Buddhist. It isn't only about doing good things. It's about how you do them. For Thich Nhat Hanh, anger at injustice was real, but acting from anger, he said, only adds more of the same to the world. So the work starts inside: a breath before the meeting, attention while you wash the dishes, listening fully to someone you disagree with. Then you go out. Not everyone in the tradition draws the lines the same way; some teachers keep monks far from politics, others step into it. But the root is old. The Buddha taught that compassion, karuna, is one of the qualities a practitioner grows. Engaged Buddhism asks where that compassion goes when you stand up from the cushion.
screen: `MONKS CHOOSE: CUSHION OR VILLAGE?` · `THEY CHOSE BOTH.` · `NOT ONLY WHAT YOU DO, BUT HOW.` · `COMPASSION OFF THE CUSHION.` · then, large: `PRACTICE IN THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: bring practice to one real problem. Sit, and take a few slow breaths. Now choose one real thing that's wrong: in your house, your street, your town, the news. Keep it small enough to hold. Notice what comes up when you think of it, maybe frustration, maybe tiredness. Breathe with that for a moment, without pushing it away. Then ask quietly: what is one thing I could do about this, from a calm place rather than an angry one? Let an answer come, or not. The bell holds the time.
Engaged Buddhism. Practice carried out of the temple and into war, peace and daily life, with attention to how the work is done. Today's word.
Your line: practice in the world. Today, take the one problem you chose, and do the first small piece of it, after one slow breath. Day one thousand nineteen.

what it means: engaged Buddhism brings practice into war, peace and daily life, with care for how the work is done.

1020.title: The Fourteenth Dalai Lama
1020.hook: a monk and teacher in exile since 1959, known for kindness as his religion
1020.howItsDone: Tibetan Buddhists attend the Dalai Lama's public teachings in Dharamsala and elsewhere, and practice compassion trainings in which they reflect that all beings want happiness and do not want suffering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, monks who left the cushion to help a village and kept practicing while they worked. Your line: practice in the world. Did you take the first small piece of your problem? Day one thousand twenty.

Ask him what he is, and the answer usually comes back simple: a Buddhist monk. Not a king, not a god-king, not a celebrity, though his face hangs in homes and on posters. A monk who gets up early, sits, studies and recites, the way monks in his tradition do. He laughs a lot in interviews, and he often brings the conversation back to one thing. When people ask about his religion, he has said it is very simple: kindness. Today is about the man in the maroon robe, and what he means by that.
screen: `A SIMPLE BUDDHIST MONK.` → `MAROON ROBES, AN EASY LAUGH.` → `HIS RELIGION: KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: In Tibetan Buddhism, the Dalai Lama is understood by his followers as a teacher who returns, life after life, as an emanation of Avalokiteshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion. Tradition says that when one Dalai Lama dies, senior lamas search for the child in whom he has returned, using signs, visions and tests. The present Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, is the fourteenth in that line. He was found as a small boy in a farming village and brought to Lhasa to be trained. Later, during the Chinese takeover of Tibet, he fled across the mountains into India. He has lived there ever since, with a community of Tibetans around him in Dharamsala, teaching, writing, and meeting people from everywhere. Not everyone sees him the same way. For Tibetans who follow him he is a spiritual guide and a symbol of their home. The government of China disputes his role. Some Tibetan Buddhists follow other lamas first. Here, though, the interest is in what he teaches. He studied the long, hard texts of Tibetan philosophy and earned the geshe degree, a title for monk-scholars. Yet when he speaks to wide audiences he keeps returning to compassion and kindness, which he calls the root of the practice, and he says these don't belong to Buddhists alone. Kindness, as he describes it, is not softness. It's training: noticing that other people want happiness and don't want to suffer, just as you do, and letting that change how you act. Practiced, again and again, until it becomes habit. That's what turns kindness from a mood into a practice.
screen: `A TEACHER WHO RETURNS.` · `FOUND AS A CHILD, TRAINED IN LHASA.` · `EXILE IN INDIA.` · `KINDNESS AS TRAINING, NOT A MOOD.` · then, large: `THEY WANT HAPPINESS TOO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: kindness as practice. Settle and breathe. Bring to mind someone you'll see today. Not your favorite person; just someone. Say to yourself, quietly: this person wants to be happy, just like me. This person doesn't want to suffer, just like me. Let that sit. Then try it with someone harder, someone who annoys you. Same two lines. Don't force a warm feeling; just notice what the words do. If the mind wanders, come back to the face and the two lines. The bell holds the time.
Tenzin Gyatso, the Fourteenth Dalai Lama, a Tibetan monk and teacher living in exile, who calls kindness the heart of his practice. Today's word.
Your line: kindness as practice. Today, when someone frustrates you, silently say: you want to be happy, just like me. Then answer them. Day one thousand twenty.

1021.title: Peace walks
1021.hook: Maha Ghosananda leads peace walks across Cambodia after the killing years
1021.howItsDone: In Cambodia, the Dhammayietra peace walks continued after Maha Ghosananda, and Buddhists elsewhere practice walking meditation, sometimes walking together in silence for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tenzin Gyatso, a monk in maroon robes who calls kindness his practice. Your line: kindness as practice. When someone frustrated you, did the words just like me come to mind? Day one thousand twenty-one.

A dirt road in Cambodia. At the front, a small, elderly monk in saffron, walking slowly, sometimes smiling, sometimes sprinkling water from a bowl on the people who kneel by the roadside. Behind him, a long line: monks, nuns, laypeople, some carrying flags, some barefoot. The fields they pass have seen terrible things. In some places there are still mines in the ground. Nobody in the line is armed. They're walking through a country that had been torn apart by its own government, and they're walking for peace. Today is the man at the front.
screen: `A DIRT ROAD, A SMALL MONK.` → `A LONG LINE BEHIND HIM.` → `NO ONE ARMED.`

segments.voice: His name was Maha Ghosananda, a Cambodian monk, and he was living abroad when the Khmer Rouge came to power. Under that regime, temples were emptied, monks were killed or forced to give up their robes, and Cambodians died in the fields and in the prisons. His students say his own family was among those lost. When the killing years ended, he went to the refugee camps along the Thai border. He set up simple temples among the tents, and there he chanted a verse from the Dhammapada that people say he repeated again and again. In Max Müller's old translation: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." He was saying it to people who had lost everything to hatred. He didn't say it to excuse what happened. He said it because, as he saw it, more hatred would only start the circle again. Later, back in Cambodia, he began leading walks for peace, the Dhammayietra, a pilgrimage of the Dhamma, through regions where fighting hadn't fully stopped. People came out of their villages to meet the walkers with water and incense. Some walkers were hurt along the way. Still they walked. His way of putting it was plain: peace is made step by step, slowly, the way you walk. Each step can be a kind of meditation, and each meditation a kind of step toward peace. He didn't promise it would be quick. He promised it would be walked.
screen: `THE KILLING YEARS.` · `CHANTING IN THE REFUGEE CAMPS.` · `HATRED CEASES BY LOVE.` · `THE DHAMMAYIETRA: WALKING FOR PEACE.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: a short walk for peace. If you can stand, stand. If you can't, sit and feel your feet on the floor. Take one unhurried step, then another, at the pace of someone in a long line. If you're seated, just press each foot gently in turn. With each step, let one quiet word ride along: peace. Not as a demand, more like company. If your mind runs ahead to your list, notice it, and come back to the next step. There's nowhere to arrive. Only this step. The bell holds the time.
Peace walks. The Dhammayietra, Maha Ghosananda's walks through a wounded Cambodia, made one slow step at a time. Today's words.
Your line: step by step, peace. Today, take a ten-minute walk somewhere ordinary, and let each step carry that one word. Day one thousand twenty-one.

1022.title: Women teaching today
1022.hook: across every school, women lead temples and teach
1022.howItsDone: Women lead Buddhist temples, monasteries, retreat centers and sitting groups in Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana communities, giving dharma talks and training students; some communities restrict certain roles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a long, unarmed line walking behind Maha Ghosananda. Your line: step by step, peace. And the week behind it: Ambedkar's vows, bhikkhuni, Dipa Ma rebuilding, monks leaving the cushion for the village, a monk who calls kindness his practice. Which one stayed with you? Day one thousand twenty-two.
screen: `STEP BY STEP, PEACE.` → `EQUAL.` · `BHIKKHUNI.` · `SHE REBUILT.` · `PRACTICE IN THE WORLD.` · `KINDNESS AS PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Long ago, the story goes, a nun named Soma sat down under a tree to meditate, and Mara, the tempter, came to shake her. A woman, he sneered, with her little bit of sense, can't reach what the sages reach. Soma didn't argue about women. She asked a better question: what does being a woman matter, when the mind is steady and wisdom is there? Mara, knowing he'd been seen through, disappeared. That conversation is very old. Today it's still going, in meditation halls, temples and monasteries, and women are the ones answering.
screen: `SOMA UNDER A TREE.` → `MARA SNEERS.` → `WHAT DOES IT MATTER, IF THE MIND IS STEADY?`

segments.voice: Soma's verses survive in the Therigatha, the verses of the elder nuns, a collection of poems by early Buddhist women about their own awakening. So women's voices are in the old canon itself. Now come forward to recent times and look across the schools. In the Theravada world, a German-born nun named Ayya Khema taught widely and helped found a place for nuns on an island in Sri Lanka. In Tibetan Buddhism, Tenzin Palmo, an English-born nun, spent years on retreat in a Himalayan cave and later built a nunnery where Tibetan nuns could study and practice. Pema Chodron, an American nun in the Tibetan tradition, became known for plain talk about fear and difficulty. In Taiwan, the nun Cheng Yen founded Tzu Chi, a Buddhist relief organization run largely by laypeople. In Zen and Korean Son, women serve as abbots and teachers, and lay women lead sitting groups in living rooms and community halls. Each of them stands in a different school, with its own rules, and they don't all agree about everything, including the ordination questions from earlier this week. But look at what they do: they run temples, give dharma talks, lead retreats, train students, and some of their students are men. So the hook's question gets its answer in practice, not in debate. That doesn't erase the obstacles women have faced, and some communities still hold back certain roles. It means the picture of Buddhist teachers as only old men in robes is out of date. Women are leading, right now, in the halls.

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like it: learn from a woman teacher, starting with Soma. Sit and breathe. Bring her to mind, under her tree, unbothered by the sneer. Now borrow her question. Notice the labels the mind keeps handing you: woman or man, young or old, good at this or hopeless at it. As each one comes up, ask it Soma's question: when the mind is steady, what does this matter? Don't argue with the label. Just let it grow smaller than the breath. When the mind wanders, come back to her question. The bell holds the time.
